lines: The shop floor asked for real-time dashboards, and the platform team built a cloud-only streaming pipeline to give it to them.
The moment the plant's own link to that cloud actually went down, every single dashboard on the floor went dark with it.
And once the link came back, the backlog that had piled up flooded straight in, keeping the dashboards stale for hours more.
Notice that neither failure was actually about the network itself being too slow; both were about what the design assumed would always be reachable.
Which two decisions, missing from that first version, would have kept the plants running and made reconnecting genuinely boring?
answer: A bigger link wouldn't have helped once it was actually down, and it does nothing at all for a backlog flooding back in.
What the plant actually needed was its own local autonomy during the outage, plus a throttle on the catch-up once the link returned.

lines: Each plant's own event rate adds up into one fleet-wide total, and a shift change or a line restart pushes that total well above its normal average.
A published compression result gets quoted here as a reference point for what's achievable, genuinely never as a promise for this particular fleet's own signals.
A gateway sitting at the edge holds every reading durably for as long as the link stays down, then forwards them back in order once it returns.
That buffer's own size is genuinely just one multiplication: how long the outage runs, times the rate it has to hold for that entire stretch.
Sensors on the floor speak in two different protocols, and the design has to decide where that translation actually happens.
A safety signal earns a stricter delivery guarantee than a routine reading does, and both still land in the very same durable log regardless.
That single log is what lets every plant stay fully decoupled from whatever happens to be consuming its data downstream.
A hot store answers an operator's question about data that's seconds old; a lakehouse holds years of history for whoever analyzes it later.
Cardinality, the sheer count of distinct series driven by labels and by how many assets actually exist, is genuinely the hot store's own limit.
That's a different constraint entirely from how much the lakehouse itself can hold, which barely cares how many distinct series feed into it.
Each reading also has to learn which machine, line, and plant it actually came from, and that join can happen early, right at ingest, or late, at read.
The plant keeps its own local broker, a short-retention store, and its own alert rules running even with the cloud link fully down.
A safety alarm earns a genuinely tighter recovery target than a quality metric does, and that difference gets written down, never assumed.
Some sites' own data genuinely has to stay put by rule, with only an aggregate ever replicated upward to the cloud.
Once the link comes back, the buffer that piled up during the outage replays straight through that very same idempotent ingest path.
A throttle on that replay is what actually keeps the catch-up itself from becoming a second outage, just shaped differently than the first one.

Notice what actually closed the gap between a plant going dark and a boring reconnect: an estimate built with a cited reference point, a buffer sized from the outage itself, and plant autonomy treated as its own degraded mode with a throttled catch-up behind it.
The sensor count across these same three plants grows by a full order of magnitude.
The WAN link itself still buffers through an outage just fine, regardless of how many sensors happen to be feeding it.
So what's actually the next bottleneck here?
answer: More sensors sending more data doesn't actually break the link, since the design already buffers straight through an outage regardless of volume.
What genuinely climbs right along with the sensor count is the hot store's own series count, against that very same label-driven limit.
